newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels free three ambassadors to mediate siege.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels free three ambassadors to mediate siege.

text.p: Leftist guerrillas, threatening to kill up to 485 hostages in the Japanese ambassador's residence, freed three ambassadors on Wednesday to negotiate the release of the captives in exchange for jailed rebels.

The guerrillas, who stormed the compound on Tuesday, called on President Alberto Fujimori to personally negotiate the release of the captives, including the Peruvian foreign and agriculture ministers and at least 12 other ambassadors from Asia, Europe and the Americas.
The rebels told local reporters from within the building that they had laid explosive booby-traps at the entrances in case police try to storm the compound.

The Cuban-inspired Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels, who are demanding the release of up to 500 jailed comrades, freed the ambassadors of Germany, Canada and Greece, a cultural attache at the French embassy and an elderly man of unknown nationality identified as Juan Kanashiro at about 6:00 p.m. EST (2300 GMT) to get the negotiations going.

"We have been freed by the (guerrillas) to serve as a contact and bridge with the Peruvian government with the aim of looking for a solution through negotiation that avoids bloodshed," Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent told reporters on his release.
"We will immediately contact the government and we have promised to maintain a personal link by telephone with the command of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA)," he added.
One hour after the three ambassadors were freed, Red Cross official Michel Minning, a Swiss national, entered the embassy residence carrying a megaphone and an envelope, witnesses said.
After about 20 minutes he left and two other Red Cross officials entered carrying supplies of food, water and an X-ray machine that they pushed on a trolley.
The evening release followed the freeing earlier on Wednesday of four elderly men. About 80 women and elderly people were released late Tuesday leaving only men as captives.
The MRTA rebels said they would kill all remaining hostages unless the government freed up to 500 jailed comrades.
"If they do not release our prisoners, we will all die in here," an MRTA guerrilla told a local radio station from within the embassy residence.
Tensions rose at noon EST (1700 GMT) when the rebels issued an ultimatum that they would kill Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela unless Fujimori joined the negotiations.
The threat came after an explosion and gunfire rocked the building but the deadline passed without incident.
MRTA rebels inside the compound accused the Peruvian government of "intransigence."

"The only solution is a political one," MRTA member Walter Loayza said, adding that the rebels wanted transportation for them and the freed prisoners to a guerrilla-controlled area in the country's jungle.
Fujimori, who suspended all public activities and called a second emergency cabinet meeting for Thursday morning, has so far not commented publicly on the attack.
Guerrilla spokesmen said they attacked the Japanese ambassador's home in protest at Tokyo's support for Fujimori, the son of Japanese immigrants, and his economic policies.

Japan was chosen as a target "due to the constant meddling of the Japanese government in Peru," the rebels said in a message sent with a released hostage, Sally Bowen, president of Peru's foreign correspondents' association.
Governments around the world urged Peru to do everything in its power to protect the hostages and not use force to flush out the rebels.

Japan, Austria, Spain, South Korea, Panama, Malaysia, Venezuela, Bolivia, Brazil, Cuba, Guatemala and Honduras confirmed their ambassadors were among the hostages. The U.S. ambassador was present at the reception but left before the attack, according to the State Department.

The drama began around 8 p.m EST (0100 GMT) Tuesday when heavily-armed rebels attacked the building, firing a rocket from outside, and around 20 rebels swarmed inside after blowing a hole in an outside wall, according to witnesses.
Some unconfirmed reports said guerrillas disguised as waiters joined the attack from the inside.
Juan Carlos Mejia, head of the special police task force handling the siege, confirmed that the rebels had smuggled in ammunition among flowers and Christmas cake.
After an initial chaotic shootout with police and security guards, there was calm for several hours while about 80 women and old people were gradually released.
One of those freed, Bowen, said the guerrillas -- dressed in black and armed with machine-guns and grenades -- were "pretty calm and determined."
But "it was scary, especially during the shooting at the beginning," she said.
As well as Tudela, the Peruvian hostages included Agriculture Minister Rodolfo Munante Sanguineti, Supreme Court President Moises Pantoja and at least three local legislators.
The rebels said they had 400 to 500 comrades in jail and their top priority was the release of their leader Victor Polay, who was imprisoned in 1992.
The attack was a major blow to Fujimori's government, which had claimed virtual victory in a 16-year war with communist rebels of the MRTA and the larger and better-known Maoist Shining Path.

The successful campaign against guerrillas has been a major factor in the return of economic stability and foreign investment. In an immediate sign of the impact of the attack, the Lima stock market suspended trading in mid-session after heavy falls.
